editorial_brief:
READER AND ANGLE. Written for a Taiwanese general reader who uses the free ChatGPT and has started to wonder what the sponsored things in it are. The question the article answers is not 'is OpenAI selling ads' - the site covered the buying side in May - but 'what is now allowed to happen inside my conversation, and does any of it reach me'. The spine is that on 2026-09-16 the ad stopped being a box beside the answer and became something a user can talk to: a sponsored agent, in a separate thread, that the user chooses to open.

THE CENTRAL FACT TO GET RIGHT. Sponsored Agents carry three limits in a single sentence - a test, with selected advertisers, in the United States - and Taiwan is not on OpenAI's published market list for ChatGPT Ads at all. Write both as statements about what OpenAI published, not as predictions. The second thing to get right is the tier rule, because it is the one line in this whole story that changes what a reader does: Free and Go see ads, Plus/Pro/Business/Enterprise/Education do not.

WHY IT MATTERS EVEN THOUGH IT IS NOT LIVE HERE. Two of the four announced changes are about the ad adapting itself to the reader: copy rewritten to fit the context of the conversation, and copy auto-translated into the user's preferred language. That means the ad a Taiwanese reader eventually sees may not be a translation anyone at the advertiser wrote or checked - and OpenAI publishes no quality control for it. That is a concrete, checkable thing to watch for, and it belongs in the piece.

SUGGESTED FIVE SECTIONS. (1) What was announced on 2026-09-16, and the one-sentence definition of a Sponsored Agent with its three limits attached. (2) The two separations OpenAI promises - distinct from ChatGPT's answers, separate from the original conversation - and the three commitments on its advertiser page; ends with the required table (max 4 columns: 項目 / 開放對象 / 地區 / 狀態; 4-6 rows covering Sponsored Agents, Ads Manager plugin, AI creative tools, text customization, HubSpot, Shopify; caption dated 2026-09-18). (3) Who sees ChatGPT ads at all: the tier rule, the market history from the running page with its update dates, and why 'not on the list' is not 'never'; diagram goes here. (4) The ad that rewrites itself: context adaptation and automatic translation, what OpenAI says the advertiser controls, and what it does not say about the translation. (5) What OpenAI did not say, and what a reader can check for themselves - the label on a sponsored conversation, the tier they are on, and the fact that this site has tested nothing.

ORIGINAL SCENARIO, to be labelled as an editorial example per BRIEF. A reader comparing two dehumidifiers taps a sponsored result and lands in a separate thread with the brand's own agent, which answers in fluent Chinese. The editorial point is not that this is sinister but that three things are true at once: the thread is not ChatGPT's own answer, the wording may have been machine-translated rather than written by the brand, and the reader chose to open it. Knowing which of the three applies is the whole skill.

TONE AND SCOPE. Plain, not alarmist, no advice about blocking or avoiding ads. Deliberately out of scope: how to buy an ad, bidding, targeting and the four-layer structure (May's article); any comparison with Google or Meta advertising (OpenAI makes none); any claim about EU or Taiwanese advertising rules; any link between Sponsored Agents and the Agents API; any hands-on impression.
